doc.title: Zeke Mullins interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 9, 2017

title: Listening to Coltrane, Bird, Dizzy and Horace Silver
summary: He listens closely to jazz greats, adapts ideas, and ties it back to altering chords as a youth.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: What do you put on, who do you listen to at home, if anybody?

Well I listen to Coltrane, I listen to Bird, Dizzy, Horace Silver — you notice only jazz musicians. Yeah, I listen to them very carefully. I don’t try to copy nothing what they’re doing but I listen very careful. If I’m going to use it I take it and turn it around just so much, so that it don’t sound like exactly what this guy’s doing.
Just like all those years ago when your father brought you that sheet music and you started like messing with it.

Yeah. Get in there with the tunes and play them down a couple of times and let me see now this first chord I think I’ll add on the ninth or add on the eleventh. But sometimes I would have to change it because some guys would say, “Listen man, that chord don’t sound just right, I don’t hear it.” I say, “All right, man, okay, all right.”

“I’ll save that for the next group I play in,” right? And see if it works there. Well I’m looking forward to hearing you later today, and I think we’ll have a good time. And it’s been fascinating talking to you.
